correctness.rationale: For an odd rung count, an independent colour class meeting consecutive rungs must meet opposite rows on those rungs. The unselected vertex across from one of these hits then has two neighbours in the class, forcing its third neighbour into the class. Repeating forces alternating selected rows around the whole cycle and violates independence on odd closure. Therefore each class occupies at most floor(n/2) rungs, and on odd n the ceiling of 2n/floor(n/2) is six at three and five at every n>=5. Even prisms are cubic bipartite, so the bipartition is a valid two-colour solution and an edge precludes one colour. On the triangular prism six distinct colours suffice. I independently generated cyclic triples for the printed blocks U^h V_5 and U^h V_7 at h=0,1,2; the union agrees with all 13 printed triples, and in each triple for each row the center, vertical neighbour and two horizontal neighbours have four different colours. Further U copies add only windows internal to the periodic block or across an already present U/U seam; the U/tail seams are unchanged. This establishes all odd n>=5 by locality, not extrapolation. The check can be replayed by zipping predecessor, center and successor in those six words cyclically and checking distinctness of those four digits. The frozen verifier and recorded output were inspected, not executed. Here n counts rungs, not vertices, and twisted ladders are outside scope.

equivalent_formulations.reasoning: On cubic graphs a strong-odd colouring either has all three neighbours equal or all three distinct at each vertex. On an odd prism the equal option would occupy the center rung and an adjacent rung with that colour, forbidden by the indexed odd-independence structure. Hence on odd prisms a strong-odd colouring is exactly a square colouring; the distinction between the two terms does not avoid overlap for the odd-parameter existence result.

value.rationale: The exact parity split is a natural classification on a standard cubic product family and is useful for testing bounded-width colouring methods. It has a structural explanation rather than a finite-list fit, and its square-colouring witness highlights a qualitative difference between even and odd rungs. This evaluates the mathematical question and result; no distinct scientific increment over the identical catalog formula and its consequences is claimed.
